name: True Green
lede: True green is the phrase books use for plain, unqualified green, and one book notes that for centuries such a green was hard to dye.

sections.title: What true means
sections.body:
The books use *true green* as an ordinary phrase, never as one named pigment [1]. Pastoureau uses it for the green of fields, woods and pasture, as opposed to the rare green gem such as the emerald that scripture mentions [2]. Coles writes that the early greens came only from copper ores such as malachite and chrysocolla, and that green and blue were often blurred [3].

Jarman uses it more narrowly. For him a true green flower is the tobacco plant's, since hellebore and hydrangea petals are not true petals [4]. The phrase is used loosely, but in these books it points to green in its plainest sense [3][4].

sections.title: A hard color to dye
sections.body:
Pastoureau stresses that dyeing in a true green was difficult for a long time [5][6]. One liturgical writer, Lothar, allowed yellow to stand in for green in exceptional cases for that reason [6]. He also notes that Judas was traditionally dressed in green, yellow or both, and floats the idea that a stage legend about actors dying in the role may trace back to a dye problem [5].

Painters and dyers often made green by mixing blue and yellow [7], and verdigris, the copper green, tended to darken with time [3]. A later change in thinking removed green from the primaries altogether [7].
